title: AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
detail:
AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool

INTC
NVDA
ORCL

Trade BTC on Coinbase

It's been said that bull markets end when good news fails to boost prices, and that bear markets end when bad news fails to send prices lower. On that note, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is 33.7% above its bear market lows in late June. Most of the high-flying artificial intelligence (AI) value-chain stocks, on the other hand -- including Intel, Oracle, Micron Technology, and Sandisk -- are down by between 20% and 62% in the same period.

There are plenty of good reasons for those stocks to be down. Yet aside from emerging factors like questionable future demand for some of the technologies those companies make, all of those players, as well as Bitcoin, have faced a constant onslaught of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty this year. Their diverging prices amid those shared headwinds mean that one thing in particular could be coming next.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Bitcoin's floor hasn't collapsed yet

Bitcoin didn't just start shrugging off bad news in the last couple of months. On Sept. 15, the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a bill intended to set rules for crypto market structures. It briefly fell below $75,000 that day, then recovered within weeks.

Then, October saw the Nasdaq Composite index fall more than 5%, as big spenders on AI failed to wow the market with their earnings reports as well as their future projections. Bitcoin dropped 10.3% in the 30-day period ending on Nov. 5, but it largely traded in a range: every daily close was between $76,198 and $84,082, regardless of what was happening in the world. That resilience had to face down a handful of problems that also weighed on tech stocks.

For instance, on Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve voted to hold interest rates steady, and the very next day's hot inflation data caused markets to expect a December hike. Rate hikes tend to be bad for risky assets like AI stocks and cryptocurrencies, as higher rates mean investors can earn a better return on low-risk Treasuries.

Before that, Brent crude oil prices climbed in October as the prospect of continued war with Iran contributed to a highly uncertain environment. Uncertainty tends to weigh on riskier assets, and rising energy costs drive inflation, which might prompt the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates further.

What Is Behind The Rebound In Qualcomm Stock?

Qualcomm (QCOM) stock gained 5.5% on Friday, November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 rose 0.3%. The company issued no announcements, earnings reports or filings that day, and four of its five peers also finished higher. Separately, Reuters reported on Friday that Alphabet disclosed a Qualcomm stake worth $548 million. Friday's gain followed a 9.5% fall on Thursday, November 5, the day after Qualcomm reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results. So what changed for chip stocks, and for Qualcomm, between Thursday and Friday?

Qualcomm Rose As Chip Stocks Recovered From A Sell-Off

Qualcomm climbed on Friday as semiconductor shares bounced back from a sell-off. A Democratic sweep of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections raised fears in the market of a slowdown in data center spending, and stocks sold off sharply on Thursday. Chip stocks were lower across the board that day. Qualcomm led the decline after its fourth-quarter results slightly beat estimates but came with light guidance. Stocks recovered some of those losses on Friday, with Nvidia, AMD and other chip manufacturers rebounding alongside Qualcomm.

A partial recovery isn't an all-clear. But a year after 21 sell-offs this sharp, the S&P 500 was higher 20 times.

These market fears reach Qualcomm because the company is building a data center business alongside its phone chips. On its November 4 call, management reiterated its $5 billion revenue target for data center in fiscal 2027. Management said most of that revenue is custom silicon for AI accelerators at two large cloud customers.

How Did Qualcomm Compare With Other Chip Makers?

Qualcomm rose more than three of the five chip makers on its peer list. Texas Instruments was the only company among the five to fall. Advanced Micro Devices posted the largest rise in the group, gaining 11.0%, while Intel also rose more than Qualcomm.

The wider technology sector advanced at a slower pace. XLK, the SPDR fund that tracks the sector, gained 1.5%, finishing well short of Qualcomm's rise. Qualcomm moved in step with its chip peers rather than on its own.

Qualcomm Stock Is Still Down Over Twelve Months

A rise of this size is not rare for Qualcomm. The stock recorded 11 sessions with a gain at least this large in the prior 365 days, and its most recent move of this magnitude in either direction was Thursday's fall.

Friday's gain still left the stock down 6.0% over twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 9.8%. Over the past six months alone, Qualcomm lost 23.8%, while the S&P 500 gained 0.25%. At $165.41, the stock closed about a third below its highest close of the past twelve months, $251.02 on May 29, 2026. It remains well above its lowest close of the year, $124.07 on April 7, 2026.

title: Here's Where I Think Intel Stock Will Be at the End of 2030
detail:
Here's Where I Think Intel Stock Will Be at the End of 2030
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 3:12 AM CST 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock has given back a huge part of its 2026 gains. Shares ended at $60.55 on Nov. 3, around 57% under the $140.94 they ended at on June 22. The stock dropped 45% in October alone.

My estimate for $5,000 put into Intel stock at that price is around $5,400 when 2030 ends. That'd be a gain of less than 10% in a bit more than four years, or under 2% a year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What surprised me is that this number assumes Intel's business does well. My estimate has Intel more than doubling its earnings per share from this year to 2030.

Most of what keeps the result down is how much investors pay for Intel's earnings today.

Image source: Intel.

Intel's profits have bounced back fast

Showing how quickly the business has turned, Intel's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share grew from $0.29 in the first quarter of 2026 to $0.42 in the second quarter and $0.52 in the third. A year before, in the third quarter of 2025, it was just $0.23. If Intel meets its fourth-quarter forecast of $0.25, its adjusted earnings per share for all of 2026 would total around $1.48 -- more than triple the $0.42 it made in 2025.

Intel's server chips are doing most of the work. Data center and AI segment revenue jumped 78% year over year to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, the segment's fastest growth in 15 years.

But that fourth-quarter forecast is a big drop from the third quarter, and PCs are the main reason. Intel expects PC unit sales industrywide to shrink around 12% this year. And it's planning for about another 10% decline in 2027. It doesn't expect PC sales to rebound for good until memory supplies improve and prices start to normalize.

What might Intel earn in 2030?

Intel's revenue may hit around $62 billion in 2026 if fourth-quarter sales land at the midpoint of its $15 billion to $16 billion forecast. This would be up about 17% over $52.9 billion in 2025.

Say revenue rises about 10% a year from there. This puts 2030 sales around $90 billion, over Intel's all-time high of $79 billion in 2021.

In the third quarter, Intel kept about 17 cents per revenue dollar as adjusted net income ($2.8 billion on $16.5 billion of revenue). I've assumed that grows to 20 cents by 2030. That's still under the more than 25 cents Intel kept in 2021. And it arguably leaves room for a foundry business that reported a $1.9 billion operating loss in the third quarter.

Investors buy both NVIDIA (NVDA) and Micron Technology (MU) to capture the spending on AI data centers: NVIDIA sells the computing systems, and Micron sells DRAM and NAND memory. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings compared with 23.4 for NVIDIA, making it look like the cheaper way in. Yet NVIDIA said in August that soaring memory prices had prompted a reset of its gross margin expectations. So will memory prices keep rising, and can NVIDIA keep growing while it pays them?

Are Memory Prices Still Rising For Micron?

They are, although Micron expects the increases to slow. During its August 26, 2026 call, NVIDIA said memory price increases had exceeded its expectations and were headed even higher. For NVIDIA, that serves as a cost warning, but for Micron, those same prices are what it sells at.

Micron provided a pricing outlook on its September 30 call. Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, compared with $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026. That forecast assumes only single-digit growth in the bits of DRAM and NAND that Micron ships, leaving price and product mix to supply the rest of the rise.

Management also said price increases would continue at a more moderate pace. Micron's 86.0% guide for its gross margin sits just below the 86.8% it reported for fiscal Q4.

Can NVIDIA Keep Growing As Memory Costs Rise?

So far it can, although its margin is slipping. NVIDIA guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2. Management expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70% and said supply, including of its new Vera Rubin systems, would remain the bottleneck through at least the end of that year.

The memory bill shows up in the margin instead. NVIDIA reported a 75.0% gross margin for fiscal Q2 and guided 74% for fiscal Q3, plus or minus half a point. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, then settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as NVIDIA's own price increases take effect.

NVIDIA's margins have also been far steadier than those of Micron. NVIDIA's operating margin averaged 61.7% over the last three twelve-month periods, compared with 35.3% for Micron. Over those periods, NVIDIA's twelve-month operating margin stayed between 58.1% and 65.2%, while Micron's twelve-month operating margin climbed from 5.2% to 74.6% in two years.

How Do NVIDIA And Micron Compare Head To Head?

Over the latest twelve months, Micron comes out ahead on growth and margin. Micron's revenue grew 256.3%, against 83.4% for NVIDIA. Its operating margin was 74.6%, compared with 65.2% for NVIDIA. Each company has debt under 1% of its market value.

Intel Corporation (INTC) stock's deep sell-off shows signs of an overreaction, in my view, as the market may be overlooking the progress the chipmaker has made in its recovery. Since its June peak, the company's market capitalization has fallen by more than half. In late October, shares cratered nearly 30% in a single session after the company issued disappointing fourth-quarter guidance. The fear now is that its recovery could take much longer than expected.

Yet isn't there some market overreaction? Despite the weak guidance, Intel delivered a solid third quarter, with 78% growth in its data center segment and significant improvements in manufacturing efficiency.

Risks remain, particularly the foundry business's heavy losses, ongoing production constraints, and massive capital spending that continues to weigh on free cash flow (FCF). Still, I see a buying opportunity after the sell-off, at the current price of $52.25. Projected 2028 adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.99 valued at a five-year average forward P/E of 27x supports an $80.73 price target, implying potential upside of 55%.

The Sell-Off Didn't Come Out of Nowhere

Intel's recent sell-off didn't happen without reason. After it released its third-quarter results on October 29, the semiconductor giant's shares plunged a staggering 28.6% in a single trading session on October 30.

Essentially, Intel provided guidance that fell well short of expectations. While Wall Street analysts projected Q4 revenue of about $17 billion, Intel's management guided to just $15 billion to $16 billion. Meanwhile, adjusted EPS guidance of $0.25 came in well below Wall Street's expectations of $0.44.

As if that weren't bad enough, management warned of production constraints, prolonged weakness in the PC market, and difficulties generating FCF in 2026. In fact, FCF was negative $1.47 billion over the last 12 months.

A Strong Quarter, but a Cloudy Outlook

At the same time, it's worth pointing out that the problem wasn't necessarily the Q3 results themselves, which, frankly, were good and even quite strong in some respects. For example, revenue and adjusted EPS rose 21% and 126%, respectively, year-over-year. Adjusted gross margin also reached 44%, up 4.1 percentage points.

Dell Sinks 16% in a Week on Intel's PC Warning. Its CFO Already Saw "Minus Double Digit" ©@Lisa Fotios from Pexels via Canva, @Lisa Fotios from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Dell Technologies (DELL) stock fell approximately 16% from October 26 to November 2, closing near $393 as higher memory costs and weakening PC demand pressured shares.

Intel (INTC) projected PC unit declines of approximately 12% in 2026 and 10% in 2027, raising concerns about a prolonged downturn.

HP (HPQ) generated approximately 75% of quarterly revenue from Personal Systems, while Super Micro Computer (SMCI) subsequently reported $19.9 billion in quarterly sales, highlighting continued AI infrastructure demand.

Dell traded at an estimated 14x forward earnings on November 2, but its $4.1 billion first-half free cash flow remains a concern despite strong server profitability.

What Happened?

Dell Technologies (DELL) stock dropped approximately 16% in the week ended November 2, falling from around $467 to $393 as investors weighed weakening PC demand against the company's expanding AI infrastructure business.

Much of the decline followed Intel's October 29 earnings discussion, when management warned that rising memory prices and supply constraints were weakening PC demand.

Intel CFO David Zinsner projected PC unit declines of approximately 12% in 2026 and another 10% in 2027, suggesting the downturn could continue into next year.

Dell had already anticipated the pressure. At Citi's September 10 technology conference, CFO David Kennedy said the PC market "is compressed for the rest of this year, like I said, minus double digit."

According to Dell's fiscal second-quarter results, Client Solutions Group contributed just 19% of segment operating income in the July quarter, down from 35% a year earlier. Infrastructure Solutions Group generated the remaining 81%.

Competitor HP faces greater PC exposure. Its fiscal third-quarter results showed $11.8 billion in Personal Systems revenue out of approximately $15.7 billion in total sales.

Dell's AI server business provides an important offset, with Infrastructure Solutions Group operating margins improving to 15.0% from 8.8% a year earlier.

Meanwhile, AI server competitor Super Micro reported $19.9 billion in quarterly sales on November 3, providing further evidence of strong infrastructure demand despite PC market weakness.

TIKR's October 27 consensus estimates projected Dell's normalized EPS increasing from $25.90 for the year ending January 2027 to $30.26 in January 2028 and $35.41 in January 2029. These forecasts predated Intel's warning.

Dell Technologies (DELL): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to January) (TIKR)
The Cash Has to Show Up on Nov. 24

Dell's biggest challenge is converting strong earnings into cash. According to its quarterly financial results, the company generated $7.6 billion in net income during the first half of fiscal 2027, compared with $4.1 billion in free cash flow.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), a data-center CPUs, GPUs, and adaptive semiconductors provider, closed at $449.04, up 11.04%. Pre-market buying followed Thursday's drop after AMD topped revenue and earnings estimates, and investors are now watching data-center demand. Trading volume reached 45.2M shares, coming in about 101% above its three-month average of 22.4M shares.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) closed at 7,379, up 0.34%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) finished at 24,579, up 1.09%. Among semiconductors spanning data-center CPUs, GPUs, adaptive computing, and embedded chips, Nvidia closed at $186.64, up 2.78%, and Intel closed at $56.28, up 7.71%, as chip buyers returned and AI demand stayed in focus.

What this means for investors

AMD seems to be benefiting from a delayed reaction to its third-quarter 2026 earnings report, which came out on Nov. 4. Investors sold off the chip stock in Thursday trading amid concerns that the midterm election results would empower politicians to regulate the industry more tightly.

Today's recovery suggests that traders may have overreacted on Thursday. Moreover, AMD delivered an objectively strong Q3 earnings report on Wednesday, reporting record revenues. The $13.4 billion in revenue was a 45% year-over-year increase, with data center revenue rising by 97% over the same period.

Additionally, analysts predict 50% revenue growth for the year, followed by an additional 79% in 2027. This suggests the AI boom is not going to end anytime soon.

Instead, where investors may have to worry is valuation. The 98 P/E ratio is well above that of its peers and may leave investors wondering whether that makes AMD stock a buy at that premium.

Indeed, buying the stock at current levels is arguably risky, as the valuation leaves investors vulnerable should unforeseen negative events occur. Nonetheless, AMD's technology places it on the cutting edge of AI, implying its long-term growth story is far from over.
